notes: Warm Up (10 mins)

🎯 Goal of this activity: To help students understand how patterns emerge from large sets of data and how those patterns influence predictions, similar to how neural networks function.

🎙️ Say: Imagine being in the world’s biggest group chat. If you had access to every message ever sent, what might you notice? What would happen if you read them all?

💬 Discuss: What would happen if you read every message ever sent in a giant group chat? 

💡 Discussion Goal: Students recognize that they would start noticing patterns, commonly used emojis, inside jokes, tone, and conversational flow. This sets up the idea that prediction is based on what comes before—just like how AI models work.

💬 Discuss: Click through the animated slide to display the prompts.
What patterns might you pick up over time?
Could you start predicting what people might say next? How?
How might your responses be shaped by what you’ve read, rather than your own original thoughts?

💡 Discussion Goal: Students should recognize how behavior can become patterned by what they've read—just like AI does. Reinforce that:
  - AI models also read (or are trained on) millions of examples.
  - AI doesn't "think," it predicts based on pattern recognition.
  - The more data it has, the better it becomes at mimicking human-like responses.

🎙️ Say: Now that we've seen how AI can predict responses based on patterns in a group chat, let's take that concept further and explore how AI models, like neural networks, make predictions with limited context and how providing more context can help improve the accuracy of those predictions.

Activity (30 mins)

Unplugged Neural Network (10 mins)

🎯 Goal of this activity: To demonstrate how neural networks predict text based on limited context and show how increasing context improves the accuracy of predictions.

☑️ Do This: Place students in groups of three to five.

📄 Distribute: Give each group one copy of the Unplugged Neural Networks activity guide, placed face down. Let students know they'll flip it over when instructed.

☑️ Do This: Introduce the activity. Make sure students understand that the purpose is to simulate how an AI model makes predictions with limited and full context.

🎙️ Say: In this activity, your group will simulate how an AI model predicts words. In Round 1, you’ll only get to see the last three words of a sentence before predicting the next word. That's how older models worked—with very limited memory. In Round 2, you'll get to see the entire previous sentence before making your prediction—like modern transformer models, which work with much more context. Let's see how that changes your predictions.

☑️ Do This: Direct students to complete Round 1 in their activity guide. Use the steps on the slide to explain the activity procedure and answer any questions. When everyone has added a word, instruct student to unfold the paper and read the full sentence aloud as a group. Have groups to compare their sentences in order to see how similar or different they were. 
For example, students' sentences could end up like this:
Space travel is 
exciting 
and 
dangerous
animals 
live.

🔁 Circulate: Circulate to ensure students aren't peeking back at earlier words or the full sentence.

☑️ Do This: Direct students to complete Round 2 in their activity guide. Use the steps on the slide to explain the activity procedure and answer any questions. When everyone has contributed, read the full sentence aloud as a group. Direct groups to compare their sentences to Round 1—how did having more context change the predictions? 
Example:
The exhausted student left school to go home to . . . rest before starting homework.
The exhausted student left school to go home to . . . eat dinner with the family.

🔁 Circulate: As students read full sentences, listen for students noticing how more words made it easier to choose a logical next word. If students aren’t making the connection, ask: "What helped you decide which word to add this time?" and "Was it easier or harder than the first round?"

Teaching Tip
Due to the variety of answers possible, there is no exemplar provided for this activity. Reference the examples above for possible student generated sentences.

💬 Discuss: Click through the animated slide to display the prompts.
How did having limited context affect predictions?
What changed when you had access to the entire starting sentence and all words that were added before you?

💡 Discussion Goal: Students recognize that limited context leads to less accurate and more random predictions, while access to more context helps predictions become more logical and connected to previous content. This mirrors how modern AI, like transformers, improves its output by analyzing longer sequences of data.

💬 Discuss: In the neural network activity, predictions improved when more context was provided. How do you think this applies to AI prompts?

💡 Discussion Goal: Students recognize that just like their own predictions, AI performs better when it has more context. The more details and structure we give in a prompt, the more accurate, relevant, and helpful the AI's response becomes. Encourage students to connect this back to their experience seeing the full sentence in Round 2.

☑️ Do This: Have students look at this slide. Explain that generative AI uses probabilities to predict what word should come next in a sentence. In this example, AI is most likely to predict the word “presents” or “eyes” next. AI is extremely unlikely to choose the word “clouds”, which is why the percentage is so small. Since this model has limited context, i.e. it only sees the words “opened their”, sometimes its predictions don’t make sense in the context of what came before it. 

Teaching Tip
Make sure students understand that the percentages represent how likely AI is to choose that word to come next. In this example, AI is most likely to choose the word “presents” (40%) next. It is slightly less likely to choose “eyes” (30%) and much less likely to choose “mail” (18%), “door” (11%), or any other word.

☑️ Do This: Have students look at this slide and note the differences between this slide and the previous slide.

💬 Discuss: Why did AI’s predictions change? How does this relate to the neuron activity? 

💡 Discussion Goal: Students should be able to explain that increased context allows AI to make more appropriate predictions. Here, the inclusion of the words “The students” led the AI to make next word predictions related to a school setting.

How LLMs Learn (10 mins)

🎯 Goal of this activity: To help students understand how large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT learn from data, recognize patterns, and refine responses through human feedback.

🎥 Video: Show the "Chatbots and Large Language Models" video (0:00-1:20).

Questions to consider with the video:
What is the difference between LLMs and typical neural networks?

Discussion Goal: Students recognize that typical neural networks perform specific tasks, while LLMs process vast text data to generate responses. LLMs predict words using probabilities, making them more flexible and capable of producing human-like text.
☑️ Do This: Define large language model.

🎥 Video: Show the "Chatbots and Large Language Models" video (1:20-1:51).

Questions to consider with the video:
Why is it important for the AI to look at longer sequences such as sentences or paragraphs? 
How does this relate to the context we provide in our prompts?

Discussion Goal: Students recognize that longer sequences provide more context, leading to more accurate predictions. They connect this to AI prompting, understanding that detailed prompts help AI generate more relevant and coherent responses.

🎥 Video: Show the "Chatbots and Large Language Models" video (1:51-2:30).

Questions to consider with the video:
How does human feedback improve AI responses? 
Why is it still important to be cautious when using AI, even with fine-tuning?

Discussion Goal: Students recognize that human feedback helps AI refine responses by correcting errors and reducing biases. They also understand that, despite fine-tuning, AI can still produce inaccurate or biased outputs, requiring users to think critically about its responses.

Prompting Challenge (10 mins)

🎯 Goal of this activity: To give students hands-on practice with AI prompting, focusing on how context, examples, and structured inputs improve AI-generated responses. Students will explore real-world career scenarios and experiment with zero-shot, one-shot, and multi-shot prompting to refine AI responses.

🎙️ Say: You've seen how AI predictions get better when given more context. Now, you're going to test that idea by giving the AI different types of prompts—starting with no example, then adding one, and finally, adding multiple examples. Try to notice how the responses change at each level.

☑️ Do This: Pair students up.

💻 Transition: Direct students to Lesson 3, Level 1 on Code Studio to complete Levels 1 through 3 of the Prompting Challenges activity. For each level, students will choose one of three options based on a real-world career path:
Level 1: Students provide a basic, unstructured prompt for their chosen career path.
Level 2: Students add one example to guide the AI's response.
Level 3: Students refine the prompt with multiple examples and structure to improve accuracy.

🔁 Circulate: Ensure students are working collaboratively with their partners and completing the Prompting Challenges section of their Unit Guide after each level, noting how the AI's responses changed and what role context played in improving them. Listen for how they describe the differences between each AI response as they add more context. Encourage students to be specific in their reflections. If students are unsure what to write, ask:
What changed in the AI’s response when you gave an example?
Did the response get more accurate, creative, or specific? How do you know?
What kind of details made the biggest difference?

Teaching Tip
Each level includes multiple career path options. If time allows, encourage students to try more than one scenario to see how prompting techniques apply across different contexts. Ask them whether their observations about AI responses stay consistent across tasks or change depending on the topic.

Assessment Opportunity
Use student reflections in the Unit Guide to assess how well students understand the role of context and structure in AI responses. Look at their answers to the reflection questions after each level (zero-shot, one-shot, and multi-shot). Based on their responses, determine next steps:
If students give vague answers or say AI's response didn't change much across levels:
Reteach the importance of context by reviewing the neural network activity analogy. Remind students that AI improves with more context and clearer instructions.
Prompt with a discussion question: "Why would AI struggle to give useful results if your prompt is too short or too open-ended?"
Small group discussion: Have students compare responses at different levels and identify specific changes in tone, structure, or accuracy.
If students show misunderstanding (e.g., they say multi-shot was worse or don't reference how examples helped):
Review sample prompt chains together as a class. Ask: "What kind of details helped this version get better?"
Have students rewrite one of their weaker prompts from earlier levels using stronger structure or clarity and re-try it with the AI.
If students clearly articulate how adding structure and examples improved the AI's response:
Move on without reteaching. These students demonstrate understanding of prompt engineering basics.
Optional Challenge: Encourage them to try a second career scenario and see if their insights apply across contexts.

💬 Discuss: What’s a creative use of this prompting technique?

💡 Discussion Goal: Students share creative ways one-shot and multi-shot prompting could be used, giving a quick snapshot of how students envision AI supporting creativity or problem-solving.

Teaching Tip
Keep it brief with popcorn-style sharing (3–4 ideas max) and note emerging themes to revisit later when discussing real-world or ethical uses of AI.
